transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Well, I guess what brings me in is that I just keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put. Like, I'll be right in the middle of a client interview—I'm a private investigator, mostly infidelity cases and some corporate background stuff. Actually, last week I had this guy who was absolutely convinced his business partner was embezzling money through a fake catering company, which is honestly a pretty clever front if you think about it, because who really audits the wholesale cost of mini quiches? 

But anyway, I'll be doing these interviews, or I'm at my tutoring sessions, or even just sitting at my weekly book club, and I just... stand up and walk away. People are really starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen. Like at book club on Tuesday, Brenda was right in the middle of talking about this mystery novel we're reading—which, to be fair, the detective in that book makes the most ridiculous rookie mistakes, like not checking the spouse's alibi first, it drives me crazy—but I just couldn't stay in my chair while she was talking. So, yeah, the sitting thing is... that's mainly why I'm here.
Over the past week or so, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable compared to your normal self?

Elevated or euphoric? No, not at all. I mean, my mood is just my normal mood. I don't think I've been unusually irritable either, which is actually kind of surprising given some of the cases I've been working lately. 

Like, I had this one surveillance job on Thursday—I was parked outside this guy's house in the suburbs for hours. And he had the most bizarre lawn ornaments. Dozens of these little ceramic frogs just staring at the street. Who collects ceramic frogs and puts them all over their front yard? It just seems like an absolute nightmare to mow around. My neighbor, Gary, has a gnome collection, and he's always complaining about the HOA getting on his case about it, but honestly, I think the HOA has a point when your yard starts looking like a miniature golf course. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my mood. Yeah, no, I feel completely normal in that department. Nothing unusual there.
When you feel the urge to get up and move, do you also notice yourself worrying excessively about things—like work, health, or other concerns—that's hard to control?

Worrying? No, not really. I mean, sure, I worry a little about work, but who doesn't? Being a P.I. is inherently unpredictable. But it's not like an overwhelming, out-of-control kind of worry. It's more just... I have this physical need to move. 

Actually, speaking of worrying about work, I was at the DMV the other day trying to pull some vehicle registration records for a skip-trace. Have you been to the DMV lately? It's like time stands still in there. And the lighting—it's that awful fluorescent hum that just drills into your skull. I was standing in line behind this woman who had a parrot on her shoulder. A literal live parrot. And nobody said a word! The clerk just stamped her paperwork like it was the most normal thing in the world. I kept trying to figure out how she got it past the security guard at the door, because usually they're so strict about everything. I mean, they made me throw away my coffee once, but a tropical bird gets a free pass? It's wild. 

But yeah, the urge to move... it's just this restless energy. It's not because I'm sitting there spinning my wheels about health or anything. I just can't stay still.
Thinking back to when you were a kid, do you remember having similar trouble sitting still, staying focused, or being easily distracted in school or at home?

Oh, wow, yeah. My mother still jokes about it. She always says I treated every single classroom like a crime scene that I just had to pace through to figure out. And honestly, she's not wrong. I remember my grade-school report cards—every single one of them said the same thing: "Bright, but can't stay in her seat," or "Needs to learn to wait her turn." 

Actually, speaking of waiting my turn, I was at the bakery this morning—the one on 4th Street with the incredible almond croissants? They have this new ticketing system, like you're at a deli counter, which is completely unnecessary for a bakery. I was holding ticket number 42, and they were on 38, and I just couldn't stand there. I ended up pacing the entire length of the pastry case, counting the different types of muffins. Did you know they make a pistachio-rose muffin now? It sounds like soap, honestly. I don't know who is buying floral-flavored baked goods. My friend Sarah tried a lavender latte once and said it tasted like drinking a candle, which is exactly what I would expect. 

But anyway, yeah, school was tough because of the sitting. I was always up and moving, just like I am now.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with pervasive, cross-situational hyperactivity (unable to remain seated during client interviews, tutoring sessions, and book club), motor restlessness (pacing at DMV, bakery), and tangential, distractible speech pattern suggestive of impulsivity/inattention. Childhood history confirms similar symptoms (report cards noting inability to stay seated, maternal observations of restlessness since school age), establishing onset prior to age 12 and chronicity into adulthood. Symptoms cause functional impairment across multiple settings (occupational, social, educational), consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
